sk: अथ हैनं शैब्यः सत्यकामः पप्रच्छ स यो ह वै तद्भगवन्मनुष्येषु प्रायणान्तमोंकारमभिध्यायीत कतमं वाव स तेन लोकं जयतीति ||
ro: atha · ha · enaṁ · śaibyaḥ · satyakāmaḥ · papraccha · saḥ · yaḥ · ha · vai · tat · bhagavan · manuṣyeṣu · prāyaṇa-antam · oṁkāram · abhidhyāyīta · katamaṁ · vāva · saḥ · tena · lokaṁ · jayati · iti ||
hi: तब शैब्य सत्यकाम ने (पिप्पलाद से) पूछा — 'भगवन्! जो मनुष्यों में मृत्यु-पर्यन्त (प्रायणान्तम् = जीवन-भर) ओंकार (ॐ) का अभिध्यान (ध्यान/उपासना) करता है — वह इसके द्वारा (तेन) किस लोक (कतमं लोकम्) को प्राप्त (जयति) करता है?'
en: Then Shaibya Satyakāma asked him: 'Bhagavan! He among men who meditates on (abhidhyāyīta) the syllable OM (oṁkāra) until death (prāyaṇa-anta) — which world (katama loka) does he win (jayati) by that?'

ws.e: until death / until the final journey

gr: The question: Satyakāma asks a practical question — not about metaphysics but about sādhana (spiritual practice): what is the fruit (phala) of meditating on OM? The question assumes lifelong practice (prāyaṇa-antam — 'until death'). oṁkāra: the syllable OM (also called Praṇava, 'that which makes new' or 'that which pervades'). It is the sonic representation of Brahman — the Māṇḍūkya Upanishad opens with 'OM ity etad akṣaram idaṁ sarvam' ('OM — this syllable is all this'). katamam lokam jayati — 'which world does he win?': the verb jayati (conquers) rather than prāpnoti (obtains) suggests active mastery, not passive reception. The answer will reveal that the 'world' depends on the depth of meditation — one, two, or three mātrās of OM.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — सत्यकाम का प्रश्न उपासना (meditation) के फल (phala) के विषय में है। 'प्रायणान्तम्' — जो जीवन-भर ओंकार का ध्यान करता है, उसका फल ध्यान की गहराई (depth) पर निर्भर है — एक मात्रा, दो मात्रा, या तीन मात्रा।
advaita.en: Shankara says Satyakāma's question is about the fruit (phala) of meditation (upāsanā). 'Prāyaṇa-antam' — for one who meditates on OM lifelong, the fruit depends on the depth of meditation — one mātrā, two mātrās, or three mātrās.
advaita.ins: OM is the simplest meditation — one syllable. But its simplicity is deceptive. You can chant OM your whole life and arrive at different destinations depending on how deeply you penetrate the syllable. The surface gives you one world; the depth gives you another.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'ओंकार अभिध्यान' = भगवान् के नाम-स्वरूप (name-form) का ध्यान। ॐ भगवान् का प्रथम नाम है — इसका जप (chanting) और ध्यान (meditation) भक्ति का सर्वोत्तम मार्ग है। 'कतमं लोकम्' — फल भक्ति की परिपक्वता (maturity) पर निर्भर है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'oṁkāra abhidhyāna' = meditation on the Lord's name-form. OM is the Lord's primary name — chanting and meditating on it is the supreme path of devotion. 'Katamam lokam' — the fruit depends on the maturity of devotion.
vishisht.ins: OM is God's first name. Before any other name — Vishnu, Shiva, Devi — there was OM. When you chant OM, you're calling God by His original name. The depth of your calling determines how close He draws you.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — ओंकार-ध्यान चेतना के ऊर्ध्वारोहण (ascent) का मार्ग है। 'प्रायणान्तम्' — यह जीवन-भर की साधना है, क्षणिक अभ्यास नहीं। ॐ की तीन मात्राएँ चेतना के तीन स्तरों (भौतिक, प्राणिक-मानसिक, आध्यात्मिक) का प्रतीक हैं।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says OM-meditation is the path of consciousness-ascent. 'Prāyaṇa-antam' — this is a lifelong practice, not a momentary exercise. The three mātrās of OM symbolise three levels of consciousness (physical, vital-mental, spiritual).
aurobindo.ins: OM is not a magic spell — it's a lifelong discipline of consciousness. The question is not 'what do I get for chanting OM?' but 'how deeply can I enter the syllable?' Depth determines destination.

dp.a: The syllable OM (also written AUM, also called Praṇava) is the most sacred sound in the Vedic tradition. It holds multiple layers of meaning: Linguistic structure: OM is composed of three mātrās (measures/components): A (अ), U (उ), and M (म). In Sanskrit phonetics, A + U naturally fuse into O (by the rule of guṇa-sandhi), so AUM becomes OM. Some traditions count a fourth element — the silence (amātra) after the M fades. Cosmological meaning: the Māṇḍūkya Upanishad identifies OM with all of reality: 'oṁ ity etad akṣaram idaṁ sarvam' — 'OM, this syllable, is all this.' The three mātrās are mapped to the three states of consciousness (A = waking, U = dream, M = deep sleep) and the three Vedas (Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma). The silence after M = turīya, the Fourth. Theological meaning: OM is the sound-form (śabda-brahman) of the formless Brahman. The Kaṭha (1.2.15-17) says: 'This syllable is indeed Brahman; this syllable is the Supreme. Knowing this syllable, one obtains whatever one desires.' Practical meaning: OM is the universal seed-mantra (bīja) used at the beginning and end of all Vedic recitation, all prayers, and all meditation. It is the 'doorway' through which consciousness passes from the mundane to the sacred.

dp.q: 🔍 Why does the question specify 'until death'?
dp.a: The phrase prāyaṇa-antam ('until death' / 'until the final departure') is significant. It specifies lifelong practice — not casual or occasional meditation. This distinguishes three levels of spiritual practice in the Upanishadic framework: (1) Occasional practice (naimittika): meditation performed on special occasions — festivals, eclipses, pilgrimages. This yields limited fruit. (2) Regular practice (nitya): daily meditation as part of one's routine. This yields greater fruit. (3) Lifelong practice (prāyaṇa-anta): unbroken meditation from initiation until death. This yields the highest fruit. The specification 'until death' also connects to the teaching on the last thought at the moment of death. The Bhagavad Gītā (8.5-6) echoes this: 'Whoever at the time of death, departing the body, remembers Me alone — he attains My being; of that there is no doubt. Whatever being one remembers at the time of leaving the body, to that very being one goes.' By meditating on OM lifelong, the practitioner ensures that OM is naturally the last thought at the moment of death — and the destination is determined by that last thought. The depth of lifelong practice determines the depth of the final meditation, which determines the 'world' attained.

sk: तस्मै स होवाच एतद्वै सत्यकाम परं चापरं च ब्रह्म यदोंकारः तस्माद्विद्वानेतेनैवायतनेनैकतरमन्वेति ||
ro: tasmai · saḥ · ha · uvāca · etat · vai · satyakāma · paraṁ · ca · aparaṁ · ca · brahma · yat · oṁkāraḥ · tasmāt · vidvān · etena · eva · āyatanena · ekataram · anveti · iti ||
hi: उनसे उन्होंने (पिप्पलाद ने) कहा — 'हे सत्यकाम! यह ओंकार (ॐ) — यह वास्तव में पर (supreme/transcendent) और अपर (lower/immanent) दोनों ब्रह्म है। इसलिए विद्वान् (ज्ञानी) इसी आयतन (आश्रय/माध्यम) से दोनों में से एक (एकतरम्) को प्राप्त करता है।'
en: To him he said: 'O Satyakāma! This syllable OM (oṁkāra) is indeed both the higher (para) and the lower (apara) Brahman. Therefore the knower (vidvān), through this very support (āyatana), reaches one or the other (ekataram).'

ws.e: by means of this support / through this medium

gr: paraṁ ca aparaṁ ca brahma — 'both the higher and the lower Brahman': Pippalāda's answer is remarkable — OM is not merely a symbol of Brahman but is Brahman in its dual aspect. Para Brahman = the unconditioned Absolute (nirguṇa), without qualities, beyond description. Apara Brahman = the conditioned Brahman (saguṇa), manifest in creation as Hiraṇyagarbha/Īśvara, with qualities. OM bridges both because it has both structure (the three mātrās A-U-M = apara, the conditioned) and silence (the amātra after M = para, the unconditioned). vidvān etena āyatanena ekataram anveti — 'the knower, through this support, reaches one or the other': the destination depends on the meditator's depth — partial understanding (one or two mātrās) reaches apara Brahman (higher worlds); complete understanding (all three mātrās with silence) reaches para Brahman (liberation). The following mantras (3-5) detail the three levels.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — ॐ एक ही है, किन्तु दो ब्रह्मों का प्रतीक है: पर ब्रह्म (निर्गुण, निराकार, अक्षर) और अपर ब्रह्म (सगुण, हिरण्यगर्भ, प्रतिष्ठित)। जिस गहराई से ध्यान करोगे, उसी स्तर का ब्रह्म प्राप्त होगा।
advaita.en: Shankara says OM is one, but symbolises two Brahmans: para (nirguṇa, formless, imperishable) and apara (saguṇa, Hiraṇyagarbha, qualified). The depth of meditation determines which Brahman is reached.
advaita.ins: OM is one door — but it opens onto two rooms. The outer room is Brahman-with-qualities: the cosmic Lord, the creator, the sustainer. The inner room is Brahman-beyond-qualities: the Absolute, the Imperishable, the nameless. How far you go depends on how deeply you enter.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — पर और अपर ब्रह्म दो पृथक् तत्त्व नहीं — एक ही भगवान् के दो पक्ष (aspects) हैं। ॐ भगवान् का सम्पूर्ण नाम है — सगुण (with attributes) और निर्गुण (beyond attributes) दोनों।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says para and apara Brahman are not two separate realities — they are two aspects of the same Lord. OM is the Lord's complete name — encompassing both saguṇa (with attributes) and nirguṇa (beyond attributes).
vishisht.ins: OM is God's full name — it contains everything He is. The manifest universe is His body; the transcendent Absolute is His essence. When you chant OM, you're addressing both aspects at once. There is no 'higher' or 'lower' God — just one God seen from two angles.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — ॐ = चेतना का सम्पूर्ण स्पेक्ट्रम (spectrum)। अपर ब्रह्म = अभिव्यक्त चेतना (manifest consciousness) — भौतिक, प्राणिक, मानसिक स्तर। पर ब्रह्म = अनभिव्यक्त चेतना (unmanifest consciousness) — अतिमानसिक (supramental) और उससे ऊपर। ॐ दोनों को जोड़ता है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says OM = the complete spectrum of consciousness. Apara Brahman = manifest consciousness — physical, vital, mental levels. Para Brahman = unmanifest consciousness — supramental and beyond. OM bridges both.
aurobindo.ins: OM spans the entire keyboard of consciousness — from the lowest physical note to the highest spiritual octave. Meditate shallowly and you reach the middle notes. Meditate deeply and you reach the highest. The syllable doesn't change — your depth does.

dp.a: The distinction between para (higher) and apara (lower) Brahman is one of the most important in Vedāntic philosophy: Para Brahman (परब्रह्म): the unconditioned Absolute. It is nirguṇa (without attributes), nirākāra (formless), nirvikalpa (without mental constructs). It cannot be described in positive terms — only through neti neti ('not this, not this'). It is pure consciousness-existence-bliss (sat-cit-ānanda) without any qualification. It is the subject of parā vidyā (higher knowledge) in Muṇḍaka 1.1.5. Apara Brahman (अपरब्रह्म): Brahman as conditioned by attributes — the cosmic Lord (Īśvara/Hiraṇyagarbha) who creates, sustains, and dissolves the universe. It is saguṇa (with attributes), accessible through worship, meditation, and devotion. It is the subject of aparā vidyā (lower knowledge) in Muṇḍaka 1.1.4. How OM bridges both: the three mātrās (A-U-M) represent the conditioned aspect — creation (A), preservation (U), dissolution (M). The silence (amātra) after M represents the unconditioned aspect — the Absolute beyond creation. Together, the sound and the silence constitute the complete Brahman. How the schools interpret this: Advaita — para Brahman alone is ultimately real; apara Brahman is a provisional description for the unenlightened. Vishishtadvaita — both are aspects of the same Lord; there is no 'lower' Brahman, only Brahman viewed from different angles. Sri Aurobindo — para is the transcendent pole and apara the immanent pole of one reality; evolution bridges them.

The word āyatana (आयतन) means 'resting-place', 'support', 'abode', or 'medium'. Calling OM an āyatana means it serves as the vehicle through which consciousness ascends to Brahman. This has practical implications: How OM works as a vehicle: (1) Sound anchors attention: the mind naturally follows sound. By focussing on OM, the mind is withdrawn from external distractions and stabilised on a single point (ekāgratā). (2) The mātrās structure the ascent: meditating on A alone reaches one level; A+U reaches a higher level; A+U+M+silence reaches the highest. The syllable itself is a 'ladder' of consciousness. (3) Vibration alters consciousness: the Vedic tradition holds that sound (śabda) is not merely heard but experienced — it has a transformative effect on the meditator's inner state. OM's particular vibration resonates with the fundamental vibration of reality (nāda-brahman). Why OM and not another mantra? The Māṇḍūkya (1) explains: 'OM is all this' — it is the universal sound that encompasses all other sounds. In Sanskrit phonetics, A is the first vowel (produced at the back of the throat) and M is the last consonant (produced at the lips). A-U-M therefore spans the entire range of human speech — it is the sound of all sounds. Any other mantra is a partial expression; OM is the totality.

sk: स यद्येकमात्रमभिध्यायीत स तेनैव संवेदितस्तूर्णमेव जगत्यामभिसम्पद्यते तमृचो मनुष्यलोकमुपनयन्ते स तत्र तपसा ब्रह्मचर्येण श्रद्धया सम्पन्नो महिमानमनुभवति ||
ro: saḥ · yadi · eka-mātram · abhidhyāyīta · saḥ · tena · eva · saṁveditaḥ · tūrṇam · eva · jagatyām · abhisampadyate · tam · ṛcaḥ · manuṣya-lokam · upanayante · saḥ · tatra · tapasā · brahmacaryeṇa · śraddhayā · sampannaḥ · mahimānam · anubhavati ||
hi: यदि वह एक मात्रा (केवल 'अ'-कार) का अभिध्यान (meditation) करे — तो वह उसी से ज्ञात होकर (संवेदित) शीघ्र ही (तूर्णम्) पृथ्वी-लोक (जगती) में पुनः जन्म लेता है (अभिसम्पद्यते)। ऋचाएँ (ऋग्वेद के मन्त्र) उसे मनुष्य-लोक में ले जाती हैं। वहाँ वह तप, ब्रह्मचर्य और श्रद्धा से सम्पन्न होकर महिमा (greatness) का अनुभव करता है।
en: If he meditates on one mātrā (the letter 'a' alone) — then, enlightened by that alone, he quickly (tūrṇam) returns to the earth (jagatī). The Ṛg Vedic verses (ṛcaḥ) lead him to the world of men (manuṣya-loka). There, endowed with tapas (austerity), brahmacarya (continence), and śraddhā (faith), he experiences greatness (mahimāna).
gr: eka-mātram = A-kāra: the first mātrā of OM, the letter A (अ). In Sanskrit, A is the most fundamental vowel — all other vowels and consonants presuppose it. Meditating on A alone is the shallowest level of OM-meditation. tūrṇam jagatyām abhisampadyate — 'quickly returns to earth': the result of one-mātrā meditation is a quick rebirth on earth — not a prolonged stay in higher worlds. However, the rebirth is elevated: the meditator returns endowed with tapas (austerity), brahmacarya (celibacy/continence), and śraddhā (faith). ṛcaḥ upanayante — 'the Ṛg verses lead him': each mātrā is associated with one of the three Vedas: A = Ṛg Veda, U = Yajur Veda, M = Sāma Veda. The Ṛg Veda's domain is the earth (bhūḥ), so A-kāra meditation leads to the earth. mahimānam anubhavati — 'experiences greatness': the same word mahimā used for the mind's creative power in dreams (4.5). Here it means an elevated human life — spiritual greatness in the earthly realm.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — एक-मात्रा (अ-कार) ध्यान = ब्रह्म-विद्या का प्रारम्भिक स्तर। इसका फल सांसारिक (worldly) है — मनुष्य-लोक में उन्नत पुनर्जन्म — किन्तु मुक्ति (liberation) नहीं। यह सिद्ध करता है कि आंशिक ज्ञान (partial knowledge) आंशिक फल (partial result) देता है।
advaita.en: Shankara says one-mātrā (A-kāra) meditation = the beginner's level of Brahman-knowledge. Its fruit is worldly — an elevated rebirth in the human world — but not liberation. This proves that partial knowledge yields partial results.
advaita.ins: If you learn only the first letter of OM, you get the first floor — a good human life. Tapas, brahmacharya, faith — these come naturally. But you're still on earth, still in the cycle. To go higher, you need the full syllable.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — एक-मात्रा ध्यान = भगवान् की बाह्य विभूति (external glory) का ध्यान। फल = तप-श्रद्धा-सम्पन्न मनुष्य-जन्म — यह भक्ति का बीजारोपण (seed-sowing) है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says one-mātrā meditation = meditation on the Lord's external glory (vibhūti). The fruit = a human birth endowed with austerity and faith — this is the seed-sowing of devotion.
vishisht.ins: Even the first step of OM-meditation isn't wasted. You come back to earth, yes — but you come back as a tapasvin, a brahmacārī, a person of faith. That's not failure. That's preparation. The next life will take you higher.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'अ'-कार ध्यान = भौतिक चेतना (physical consciousness) का शुद्धिकरण (purification)। फल = पृथ्वी-लोक में एक उन्नत जीवन — तप, ब्रह्मचर्य, श्रद्धा ये भौतिक स्तर के सर्वोत्तम गुण हैं।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says A-kāra meditation = purification of the physical consciousness. The fruit = an elevated life on earth — tapas, brahmacharya, faith are the highest qualities of the physical plane.
aurobindo.ins: A is the ground floor of OM — the physical, the earthly. Meditating on it purifies your material nature. You come back to earth, but transformed: disciplined, continent, faithful. That's the highest expression of the physical plane.

dp.q: 🔍 The three mātrās and their cosmic correspondences
dp.a: The Prashna Upanishad maps the three mātrās (components) of OM to three ascending levels: (1) A-kāra (अ) — first mātrā: corresponds to the Ṛg Veda, the earth (bhūḥ), the waking state, and the world of men (manuṣya-loka). The letter A is the most basic vowel — it is present in the pronunciation of every other letter. It represents the foundation — the material, the manifest, the beginning. Meditating on A alone yields an elevated human rebirth. (2) U-kāra (उ) — second mātrā: corresponds to the Yajur Veda, the mid-region (bhuvaḥ/antarikṣa), the dream state, and the lunar world (soma-loka/candra-loka). U is the intermediary vowel — higher than A but not the pinnacle. It represents the subtle, the transitional, the interior. Meditating on A+U yields ascent to the lunar world with eventual return. (3) M-kāra (म) — third mātrā: corresponds to the Sāma Veda, the heaven (svaḥ), the deep sleep state, and the solar world (sūrya-loka/brahma-loka). M is the terminal consonant — the closing of the lips, the culmination. It represents the causal, the complete, the resolution. Meditating on all three mātrās together yields ascent to the world of Brahman with the possibility of full liberation. These correspondences are not arbitrary but follow the phonetic progression of OM: A (throat-open, expansive) → U (throat-narrowing, ascending) → M (lips-closing, culminating) → silence (beyond sound, transcendent).

dp.q: 🔍 Tapas, Brahmacharya, and Shraddha — the three spiritual foundations
dp.a: The mantra lists three qualities that characterise the elevated human rebirth attained by A-kāra meditation: (1) Tapas (तपस्) — austerity, inner heat, disciplined effort. From √tap (to heat/burn). Not mere physical penance but the focused intensity of spiritual practice. Tapas burns away impurities (kleśas) and generates the 'heat' that transforms the practitioner. The Taittirīya (3.2-6) identifies tapas as the method by which Bhṛgu discovers the five sheaths of Brahman. (2) Brahmacharya (ब्रह्मचर्य) — literally 'walking in Brahman' or 'conduct befitting Brahman'. Conventionally, it means celibacy/sexual continence, but in its deeper sense it means directing all energy toward Brahman rather than dissipating it in sensory indulgence. The Upanishadic student (brahmacārin) lives with the teacher, studies the Vedas, and channels all vitality into learning. (3) Śraddhā (श्रद्धा) — faith, trust, conviction. Not blind belief but deep confidence in the reality of what the Upanishads teach — confidence that Brahman exists, that the Self is Brahman, and that meditation leads to realisation. The Chāndogya (7.19) says: 'When one has śraddhā, one meditates; without śraddhā, one does not meditate.' These three form a spiritual triangle: tapas provides the energy, brahmacharya provides the discipline, and śraddhā provides the direction. Together, they make the human life a preparation for higher attainment in future lives.

sk: अथ यदि द्विमात्रेण मनसि सम्पद्यते सो ऽन्तरिक्षं यजुर्भिरुन्नीयते सोमलोकम् स सोमलोके विभूतिमनुभूय पुनरावर्तते ||
ro: atha · yadi · dvi-mātreṇa · manasi · sampadyate · saḥ · antarikṣaṁ · yajurbhiḥ · unnīyate · soma-lokam · saḥ · soma-loke · vibhūtim · anubhūya · punaḥ · āvartate ||
hi: और यदि वह दो मात्राओं (अ + उ) से मन में (ध्यान) सम्पन्न हो — तो वह अन्तरिक्ष (mid-region) में यजुर्वेद (के मन्त्रों) द्वारा ले जाया जाता है — सोम-लोक (चन्द्र-लोक) को। वह सोम-लोक में विभूति (divine glory / ऐश्वर्य) का अनुभव करके पुनः लौटता है (पुनरावर्तते)।
en: And if he meditates with two mātrās (A + U) — he is elevated in the mind to the mid-region (antarikṣa), led upward by the Yajur Vedic verses (yajurbhiḥ) to the world of the moon (soma-loka). Having experienced glory (vibhūti) in the soma-loka, he returns again (punar āvartate).

ws.h: पुनः लौटता है / वापस आता है

gr: dvi-mātreṇa = A + U: the first two mātrās of OM. When A and U combine by sandhi, they produce the O-sound. This is a deeper level of meditation than A alone. soma-loka: the lunar world — associated with the pitṛyāna (path of the ancestors) described in Prashna 1.9 and Chāndogya 5.10. The meditator on two mātrās reaches the moon-world (a higher realm than earth) but returns (punar āvartate). punar āvartate — 'returns again': the crucial limitation. Two-mātrā meditation is insufficient for liberation. The meditator enjoys divine glory (vibhūti) in the soma-loka but eventually exhausts the merit and returns to the cycle of birth-death-rebirth. This echoes the Bhagavad Gītā (9.21): 'Having enjoyed the vast heavenly world, they return to the mortal realm when their merit is exhausted.' yajurbhiḥ: the Yajur Veda 'conducts' the meditator upward, just as the Ṛg Veda conducted the one-mātrā meditator to earth. The association is: Ṛg = earth, Yajur = mid-region, Sāma = heaven.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — द्वि-मात्रा ध्यान = मध्यम स्तर। फल = सोम-लोक (चन्द्र-लोक) — दिव्य विभूति (divine glory) का अनुभव — किन्तु 'पुनरावर्तते' — लौटना पड़ता है। यह सगुण ब्रह्म (अपर ब्रह्म) की उपासना का फल है — उच्च किन्तु अस्थायी।
advaita.en: Shankara says two-mātrā meditation = the intermediate level. Fruit = soma-loka (lunar world) — experience of divine glory — but 'punar āvartate' — one must return. This is the fruit of saguṇa Brahman (apara Brahman) worship — elevated but temporary.
advaita.ins: Two mātrās take you higher — to the moon, to divine glory, to the realm of the ancestors. But the ticket is round-trip. You enjoy the splendour, your merit runs out, and you return. Beautiful scenery, temporary visa.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — सोम-लोक = भगवान् की विभूति (divine glory) का अनुभव-स्थान। 'पुनरावर्तते' — लौटना इसलिए कि भक्ति अभी पूर्ण (complete) नहीं — प्रपत्ति (complete surrender) अभी शेष है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says soma-loka = the realm where the Lord's vibhūti (divine glory) is experienced. 'Punar āvartate' — the return is because devotion is not yet complete — prapatti (complete surrender) remains to be attained.
vishisht.ins: You reach God's glory but not God's feet. The moon-world shows you His splendour — but seeing splendour is not the same as surrendering to Him. You return because the surrender is incomplete.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'अ + उ' ध्यान = भौतिक + प्राणिक-मानसिक चेतना का शुद्धिकरण। फल = सूक्ष्म लोक (subtle world) — विभूति का अनुभव — किन्तु अतिमानसिक (supramental) स्तर तक नहीं पहुँचा, इसलिए लौटना पड़ता है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says A+U meditation = purification of physical + vital-mental consciousness. Fruit = the subtle world (soma-loka) — experience of vibhūti — but not reaching the supramental level, hence the return.
aurobindo.ins: Two mātrās take you to the second floor — the subtle, the vital-mental. You see divine glory there. But you haven't reached the top floor — the supramental. And what goes up without reaching the summit must come down.

dp.a: The soma-loka (world of the moon / lunar sphere) is one of the most frequently mentioned celestial destinations in the Upanishads: Cosmological location: in Vedic cosmology, the soma-loka is the mid-region (antarikṣa) between earth (bhūḥ) and heaven (svaḥ). The moon (Soma/Candra) presides over this realm. It is higher than the earth but lower than the sun (sūrya-loka / brahma-loka). Who goes there? Those who follow the pitṛyāna ('path of the ancestors'): people who have performed good karma — rituals, charity, public service — but have not attained the liberating knowledge of Brahman. In the Prashna's framework, those who meditate on two mātrās of OM. What happens there? The soul enjoys the vibhūti (divine glory) accumulated through its good deeds. This enjoyment is real but finite — it lasts only as long as the accumulated merit (puṇya) lasts. The return: when the merit is exhausted, the soul 'returns' (punar āvartate) — it descends through rain, enters food, enters a new body, and is reborn. This process is described in detail in Chāndogya 5.10.5-6: 'From the ether (ākāśa) they pass to air (vāyu), from air to rain (varṣa), from rain to earth (pṛthivī), from earth to food (anna), from food to semen (retas), from semen to a new body.' The lesson: the soma-loka is good but not ultimate. It is a temporary reward, not liberation. Only the three-mātrā meditation (the full OM with silence) leads to non-return.

The phrase punar āvartate ('returns again') is one of the most significant in Upanishadic soteriology. It marks the boundary between temporary attainment and permanent liberation: The problem of return: in the Vedic worldview, even the highest heavenly worlds are temporary. Good karma takes you up; when the karma is exhausted, you come back down. The Bhagavad Gītā (8.16) states this definitively: 'From the world of Brahmā downward, all worlds are subject to return, O Arjuna. But having attained Me, there is no rebirth.' Why does the two-mātrā meditator return? Because two-mātrā meditation reaches apara Brahman (the conditioned, qualified Brahman) — a realm of glory and power, but still within the domain of creation. Anything within creation is subject to time, change, and dissolution. Only para Brahman (the unconditioned Absolute) is beyond time — and reaching it requires the complete three-mātrā meditation with the understanding of silence. The hierarchy of non-return: (1) One mātrā → earth (manuṣya-loka) → returns quickly. (2) Two mātrās → moon (soma-loka) → returns after enjoying vibhūti. (3) Three mātrās → sun (brahma-loka) → does NOT return (described in next mantra). The practical implication: partial practice yields partial results. The Upanishad is not discouraging partial practice — even one mātrā yields an elevated rebirth — but it is encouraging the aspirant to go all the way. The full syllable, fully understood, is the only path to non-return.

sk: यः पुनरेतं त्रिमात्रेणोमित्येतेनैवाक्षरेण परं पुरुषमभिध्यायीत स तेजसि सूर्ये सम्पन्नो यथा पादोदरस्त्वचा विनिर्मुच्यते एवं ह वै स पाप्मना विनिर्मुक्तः स सामभिरुन्नीयते ब्रह्मलोकम् स एतस्माज्जीवघनात्परात्परं पुरिशयं पुरुषमीक्षते तदेतौ श्लोकौ भवतः ||
ro: yaḥ · punaḥ · etaṁ · tri-mātreṇa · om · iti · etena · eva · akṣareṇa · paraṁ · puruṣam · abhidhyāyīta · saḥ · tejasi · sūrye · sampannaḥ · yathā · pādodaraḥ · tvacā · vinirmucyate · evaṁ · ha · vai · saḥ · pāpmanā · vinirmuktaḥ · saḥ · sāmabhiḥ · unnīyate · brahma-lokam · saḥ · etasmāt · jīva-ghanāt · parāt-paraṁ · puriśayaṁ · puruṣam · īkṣate · tat · etau · ślokau · bhavataḥ ||
hi: जो फिर इस तीन-मात्रा (अ + उ + म) ओम् — इस अक्षर से — पर पुरुष (Supreme Person) का अभिध्यान (ध्यान) करे — वह तेज (प्रकाश) में, सूर्य में सम्पन्न हो जाता है। जैसे साँप (पादोदर) अपनी त्वचा (केंचुली) से छूट जाता (विनिर्मुच्यते) है — वैसे ही वह पाप (pāpman) से विनिर्मुक्त हो जाता है। वह साम-वेद (के मन्त्रों) द्वारा ब्रह्म-लोक को ले जाया जाता है। वह इस जीव-घन (जीवों के समूह / शरीर-बद्ध जीव) से (ऊपर उठकर) परात्पर (Supreme beyond the supreme) पुरिशय (शरीर-नगर में शयन करने वाले) पुरुष को देखता (ईक्षते) है। इस विषय में ये दो श्लोक हैं —
en: But he who meditates on the Supreme Person (para puruṣa) with this syllable OM of three mātrās (A + U + M) — he is united with the light (tejas), the sun (sūrya). As a snake (pādodara) is freed from its skin (tvacā) — so is he freed from sin (pāpman). He is led upward by the Sāma Vedic hymns (sāmabhiḥ) to the world of Brahman (brahma-loka). From this mass of living beings (jīva-ghana) he sees the Supreme Person (parāt-para puruṣa), who dwells in the city (puriśaya). Regarding this, there are these two verses —

ws.h: तीन मात्राओं से / अ + उ + म
त्वचा (केंचुली) से छूट जाता है / मुक्त हो जाता है
जीवों के समूह/घन से / शरीर-बद्ध जीवों के सम्मिलन से
ws.e: from the mass of living beings

ws.h: परात्पर / परम से भी परम / सर्वोच्च
पुर (शरीर-नगर) में शयन करने वाला / निवास करने वाला

gr: tri-mātreṇa = A + U + M: the complete OM — all three mātrās meditated upon as one syllable directed toward the Supreme Person (para puruṣa). This is the deepest level of meditation. The snake-skin simile: pādodaraḥ tvacā vinirmucyate — 'as a snake is freed from its skin'. The snake doesn't fight its old skin — it simply grows beyond it, and the old skin falls away. Similarly, the three-mātrā meditator doesn't 'fight' sin — he grows beyond it, and sin falls away naturally. sāmabhiḥ unnīyate brahma-lokam — 'led by Sāma hymns to brahma-loka': completing the Vedic correspondence — A/Ṛg/earth, U/Yajur/antarikṣa, M/Sāma/brahma-loka. The Sāma Veda, associated with chanting and melody, leads to the highest realm. jīva-ghanāt parāt-paraṁ puriśayaṁ puruṣam īkṣate — 'from the mass of jīvas, he sees the Supreme Person who dwells in the city': the culminating vision. The liberated one rises above the aggregate of embodied souls and perceives the parāt-para puruṣa — the Supreme beyond the supreme — who dwells in the 'city' (pura = body). puriśaya = 'city-dweller' — an etymology of 'puruṣa' (puri + śaya = one who lies in the city/body).

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — तीन-मात्रा ध्यान = पूर्ण ओंकार-विद्या। 'परात्परं पुरुषम् ईक्षते' — वह पर ब्रह्म (nirguṇa) को देखता है — ज्ञान (knowledge) से पाप-रूपी केंचुली गिर जाती है — और ब्रह्म-लोक में क्रम-मुक्ति (gradual liberation) या सद्यो-मुक्ति (immediate liberation) प्राप्त होती है।
advaita.en: Shankara says three-mātrā meditation = complete OM-knowledge. 'Parāt-paraṁ puruṣam īkṣate' — he sees the Supreme Brahman (nirguṇa). Through knowledge, the snake-skin of sin falls away, and in brahma-loka he attains krama-mukti (gradual liberation) or sadyo-mukti (immediate liberation).
advaita.ins: Three mātrās, fully understood — that's the whole OM. The whole syllable, aimed at the Supreme. Sin drops off like a snake's old skin — not by fighting it but by outgrowing it. And then you see what was always there: the Self beyond all selves.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'परात्परं पुरिशयं पुरुषम्' — यह भगवान् नारायण हैं जो प्रत्येक जीव के हृदय-गुहा (heart-cave) में निवास करते हैं। तीन-मात्रा ध्यान से भक्त ब्रह्म-लोक (वैकुण्ठ) में भगवान् का साक्षात् दर्शन प्राप्त करता है — और फिर कभी नहीं लौटता।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'parāt-paraṁ puriśayaṁ puruṣam' = Lord Nārāyaṇa who dwells in the heart-cave of every being. Through three-mātrā meditation, the devotee reaches brahma-loka (Vaikuṇṭha), attains direct vision of the Lord, and never returns.
vishisht.ins: Three mātrās take you all the way — to the Lord's own world. And there, for the first time, you see Him face to face — the Person who was always living in your heart. The snake-skin of sin was blocking the view. Now it's gone.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'त्रि-मात्रा' = भौतिक + प्राणिक-मानसिक + आध्यात्मिक चेतना — सम्पूर्ण स्पेक्ट्रम। 'पादोदर-उपमा' — पुरानी चेतना (old consciousness) से मुक्ति — जैसे साँप केंचुली त्यागता है। 'परात्पर पुरुष' = अतिमानसिक पुरुष (Supramental Being) — चेतना के ऊर्ध्वारोहण का शिखर।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'tri-mātrā' = physical + vital-mental + spiritual consciousness — the complete spectrum. The snake-skin simile = liberation from the old consciousness. 'Parāt-para puruṣa' = the Supramental Being — the summit of consciousness-ascent.
aurobindo.ins: Three mātrās span the entire range: body, mind, spirit. When all three are purified and unified through OM, the old consciousness drops away like a dead skin. What emerges is a new being — one who can see the Supreme Person face to face.

dp.a: The snake-skin simile (pādodara-upamā) is one of the most elegant images for liberation in the Upanishads: The image: a snake (pādodara, literally 'belly-footed') naturally sheds its old skin as it grows. The old skin doesn't need to be 'fought' or 'destroyed' — the snake simply outgrows it, and it falls away. The new snake emerges clean, glistening, renewed. The application: the meditator who practises the full three-mātrā OM doesn't need to 'fight' sin (pāpman). Through deep meditation, he outgrows sin — the old karmic residue falls away naturally, like the old skin. This is significant because it presents liberation not as a battle but as a natural growth process. You don't defeat sin; you transcend it. Why a snake? The snake is a powerful symbol in Indian tradition: (1) It renews itself — shedding skin suggests immortality (the snake appears to be 'reborn'). (2) It is close to the earth — the 'belly-footed' creature represents the soul bound to the material world. (3) The shedding is complete — the old skin comes off in one piece, leaving nothing behind. Similarly, liberation is total — not partial cleaning but complete freedom. Other Upanishadic occurrences: The Chāndogya (5.10.10) uses the same image in the context of the devayāna path, and the Bṛhadāraṇyaka (4.4.7) uses a similar image of the Self shedding the body at death.

dp.q: 🔍 Brahma-loka and the hierarchy of destinations
dp.a: The Prashna Upanishad establishes a clear three-tier hierarchy of destinations based on the depth of OM-meditation: Tier 1: Manuṣya-loka (world of men) — attained by one-mātrā (A) meditation. The meditator returns to earth quickly, reborn with spiritual qualities (tapas, brahmacharya, śraddhā). This is a good human life but still within saṁsāra. Associated with the Ṛg Veda. Tier 2: Soma-loka (world of the moon) — attained by two-mātrā (A+U) meditation. The meditator experiences divine glory (vibhūti) in the lunar sphere but returns (punar āvartate) when the merit is exhausted. This corresponds to the pitṛyāna (path of the ancestors). Associated with the Yajur Veda. Tier 3: Brahma-loka (world of Brahman) — attained by three-mātrā (A+U+M) meditation. The meditator is freed from sin (pāpman), reaches the solar sphere, and sees the Supreme Person (parāt-para puruṣa). From brahma-loka there is no return. This corresponds to the devayāna (path of the gods). Associated with the Sāma Veda. Is brahma-loka the same as liberation? There are two views: (1) Krama-mukti (gradual liberation): the soul reaches brahma-loka and attains final liberation there at the end of the cosmic cycle (pralaya), without returning to earth. This is Rāmānuja's view. (2) Sadyo-mukti (immediate liberation): the three-mātrā meditation, when combined with true knowledge (jñāna), leads directly to liberation, with brahma-loka being a metaphor for the liberated state. This is Shankara's preferred interpretation for the fully enlightened.

sk: तिस्रो मात्रा मृत्युमत्यः प्रयुक्ता अन्योन्यसक्ताः अनविप्रयुक्ताः क्रियासु बाह्याभ्यन्तरमध्यमासु सम्यक्प्रयुक्तासु न कम्पते ज्ञः ||
ro: tisraḥ · mātrāḥ · mṛtyu-matyaḥ · prayuktāḥ · anyonya-saktāḥ · anaviprayuktāḥ · kriyāsu · bāhya-abhyantara-madhyamāsu · samyak · prayuktāsu · na · kampate · jñaḥ ||
hi: तीन मात्राएँ — जो मृत्यु-मती (मृत्यु-संयुक्त / मृत्यु के अधीन) हैं — जब (पृथक्-पृथक्) प्रयुक्त (employed) की जाएँ — परस्पर सक्त (attached) किन्तु अविप्रयुक्त (unseparated) — (और जब) बाह्य (external), आभ्यन्तर (internal), और मध्यम (intermediate) क्रियाओं में सम्यक् (rightly) प्रयुक्त हों — तब ज्ञ (the knower) कम्पित नहीं होता (na kampate) — अर्थात् अचल (unshaken) रहता है।
en: The three mātrās, when employed separately, are subject to death (mṛtyu-matyaḥ). But when joined together — mutually connected (anyonya-saktāḥ) and unseparated (anaviprayuktāḥ) — and rightly employed (samyak prayuktāsu) in the three activities — external (bāhya), internal (abhyantara), and intermediate (madhyama) — then the knower (jña) is not shaken (na kampate).

ws.h: परस्पर जुड़ी हुई / एक-दूसरे से सक्त

ws.e: in the external, internal, and intermediate activities

gr: mṛtyu-matyaḥ prayuktāḥ — 'when employed separately, subject to death': if A, U, and M are meditated upon individually (as in mantras 3-5), the results are mortal — rebirth on earth (A) or in soma-loka (A+U). Only the complete, unified OM leads beyond death. anyonya-saktāḥ anaviprayuktāḥ — 'mutually connected and unseparated': the three mātrās must be understood as one indivisible whole, not three separate components. This echoes the Māṇḍūkya's treatment: A, U, M are not three syllables but three 'feet' (pāda) of one reality. bāhya-abhyantara-madhyama — three domains of practice: (1) bāhya (external) = Vedic recitation (uccāraṇa), physical posture, ritual; (2) abhyantara (internal) = mental meditation, contemplation; (3) madhyama (intermediate) = prāṇāyāma, breath-regulation — which bridges the physical and the mental. na kampate jñaḥ — 'the knower is not shaken': the culminating statement. When OM is practised as a unified whole across all three domains, the knower becomes acala (immovable) — established in Brahman, undisturbed by life's changes.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — पृथक्-पृथक् मात्राओं का ध्यान 'मृत्युमत्' (मृत्यु-अधीन) है — केवल सांसारिक फल। जब तीनों मात्राएँ एक अविभाज्य ओंकार (indivisible OM) के रूप में ध्यान की जाएँ — बाह्य, आन्तरिक, मध्यम तीनों क्रियाओं में — तब ज्ञानी अचल (unshakeable) हो जाता है — मृत्यु उसे कम्पित नहीं कर सकती।
advaita.en: Shankara says meditating on mātrās separately is 'mṛtyu-mat' (subject to death) — yielding only worldly results. When all three mātrās are meditated upon as one indivisible OM — in all three domains of practice (external, internal, intermediate) — the knower becomes unshakeable — death cannot touch him.
advaita.ins: OM has three parts, but it's one syllable. If you break it apart — A here, U there — you get fragments, and fragments belong to the mortal world. Unite them. Let A flow into U flow into M flow into silence. Then the syllable is whole, and you are whole, and nothing can shake you.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'अन्योन्यसक्ताः अनविप्रयुक्ताः' — तीन मात्राएँ भगवान् के तीन पक्षों (aspects) का प्रतीक हैं — सृष्टि (A), स्थिति (U), संहार (M) — जो भगवान् में अविभाज्य (inseparable) हैं। सम्यक् ध्यान = भगवान् को उनकी सम्पूर्णता (totality) में जानना।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'anyonya-saktāḥ anaviprayuktāḥ' — the three mātrās symbolise the Lord's three aspects — creation (A), preservation (U), dissolution (M) — which are inseparable in the Lord. Right meditation = knowing the Lord in His totality.
vishisht.ins: God creates, sustains, and dissolves — three functions, one God. If you worship only the Creator or only the Sustainer, you know a fragment. Unite all three — see the full God — and you become unshakeable.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'बाह्य, आभ्यन्तर, मध्यम' = शारीरिक (physical), मानसिक (mental), प्राणिक (vital) — तीन स्तरों पर ओंकार-साधना। जब तीनों स्तर एकीकृत (integrated) हों — 'न कम्पते ज्ञः' — चेतना सुदृढ़ (firmly established) हो जाती है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'bāhya, abhyantara, madhyama' = physical, mental, vital — OM-practice at three levels. When all three levels are integrated — 'na kampate jñaḥ' — consciousness becomes firmly established.
aurobindo.ins: OM must pervade your whole being — body, breath, and mind. If your lips chant OM but your mind wanders, the practice is partial. If your mind contemplates OM but your breath is chaotic, it's still incomplete. Integrate all three, and you become a mountain.

dp.q: 🔍 Why is separate meditation 'subject to death'?
dp.a: The phrase mṛtyu-matyaḥ prayuktāḥ ('when employed separately, subject to death') teaches a crucial lesson about the nature of spiritual practice: The principle: partial practice yields partial results — and all partial results are temporary (mortal). Only complete practice yields complete results (liberation from death). Why? When A is meditated upon alone, the meditator connects with one level of reality (the physical/earth). When A+U are meditated upon, the meditator connects with two levels (physical + subtle/moon). But reality is not fragmented — Brahman is an indivisible whole. To connect with reality as it truly is, one must meditate on the whole OM — all three mātrās plus the silence. A fragmented meditation connects with a fragmented reality — and any fragment of reality is within creation, within time, within death. The three domains: the verse also insists that OM be 'rightly employed' (samyak prayuktāsu) in three domains: (1) Bāhya (external) — physical chanting, ritual, posture. The body participates. (2) Abhyantara (internal) — mental contemplation, understanding the meaning, meditating on Brahman. The mind participates. (3) Madhyama (intermediate) — breath-regulation (prāṇāyāma), linking body and mind. The vital breath participates. When all three domains are unified under one practice — the knower (jña) 'is not shaken' (na kampate). This is the Upanishadic equivalent of integral practice — body, breath, and mind working together.

The image of the unshakeable knower (na kampate jñaḥ) represents the culmination of OM-meditation: What 'shakes' a person? In ordinary life, a person is shaken by: pleasure and pain (sukha-duḥkha), praise and blame (yaśa-apayaśa), gain and loss (lābha-alābha), birth and death (janma-mṛtyu). These are the 'pairs of opposites' (dvandva) that keep consciousness oscillating. What makes the knower unshakeable? The complete OM-meditation establishes the knower in the ground of all three states — waking (A), dream (U), deep sleep (M), and the silence beyond (turīya). One who is established in the ground cannot be shaken by what happens in any particular state — just as the earth is not shaken by the weather that passes over it. Parallel concepts: (1) The Bhagavad Gītā's sthita-prajña (person of steady wisdom, 2.56): 'He whose mind is undisturbed in sorrows and free from desire in pleasures, from whom passion, fear, and anger have departed — he is called a sage of steady wisdom.' (2) The Kaṭha's (2.3.1) aśvattha-vṛkṣa (eternal fig tree) rooted in Brahman — unshakeable because its root is the Absolute. (3) The Yogic samādhi — the state where consciousness is so firmly established in its object that it cannot be disturbed. The 'unshakeable knower' is not stoic or emotionless — he is simply rooted. Events happen, emotions arise, but his centre does not move because his centre is Brahman.

sk: ऋग्भिरेतं यजुर्भिरन्तरिक्षं सामभिर्यत्तत्कवयो वेदयन्ते तमोंकारेणैवायतनेनान्वेति विद्वान्यत्तच्छान्तमजरममृतमभयं परं चेति ||
ro: ṛgbhiḥ · etaṁ · yajurbhiḥ · antarikṣaṁ · sāmabhiḥ · yat · tat · kavayaḥ · vedayante · tam · oṁkāreṇa · eva · āyatanena · anveti · vidvān · yat · tat · śāntam · ajaram · amṛtam · abhayaṁ · paraṁ · ca · iti ||
hi: ऋचाओं (Ṛg) से इस (पृथ्वी-लोक) को, यजुर्वेद (मन्त्रों) से अन्तरिक्ष को, साम (मन्त्रों) से जो उस (ब्रह्म-लोक) को — कवि (seers / ज्ञानी) जानते हैं — उसे ओंकार आयतन (OM = support/vehicle) से ही विद्वान् प्राप्त करता है — जो शान्त (śānta), अजर (ageless), अमृत (immortal), अभय (fearless), और पर (supreme) है — वही (परब्रह्म है)।
en: By the Ṛg verses — this (earth); by the Yajur verses — the mid-region (antarikṣa); by the Sāma verses — that which the seers (kavayaḥ) know. Through the syllable OM alone — through this support (āyatana) — the knower (vidvān) reaches that which is peaceful (śānta), ageless (ajara), immortal (amṛta), fearless (abhaya), and supreme (para).
gr: The concluding verse: this mantra summarises the entire teaching of Question 5. The three Vedas lead to three worlds: Ṛg → earth, Yajur → mid-region, Sāma → that which the seers know (brahma-loka). But OM alone — as the unified āyatana (support) — leads to the ultimate reality. Five attributes of Brahman: (1) śānta (peaceful) — beyond all disturbance; (2) ajara (ageless) — beyond time; (3) amṛta (immortal) — beyond death; (4) abhaya (fearless) — beyond all fear; (5) para (supreme) — beyond everything else. This five-fold description is a classic Upanishadic way of describing Brahman by negating the qualities of saṁsāric existence: saṁsāra is agitated → Brahman is śānta; saṁsāra involves aging → Brahman is ajara; saṁsāra ends in death → Brahman is amṛta; saṁsāra is pervaded by fear → Brahman is abhaya; saṁsāra is limited → Brahman is para. kavayaḥ vedayante — 'the seers know': Brahman is known not by logical argument or sensory observation but by direct seeing (sākṣātkāra). The kavi is not a philosopher but a seer — one whose inner eye has opened.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — ऋग्-यजुः-सामवेद क्रमशः भू-लोक, अन्तरिक्ष, और ब्रह्म-लोक तक ले जाते हैं — किन्तु इन सबसे परे जो शान्त-अजर-अमृत-अभय-पर ब्रह्म है — वह केवल ओंकार-विद्या (OM-knowledge) से प्राप्त होता है। ओंकार = ब्रह्म-विद्या का द्वार।
advaita.en: Shankara says the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas lead respectively to earth, mid-region, and brahma-loka — but the Brahman that is beyond all these — śānta, ajara, amṛta, abhaya, para — is reached only through OM-knowledge. OM = the gateway to Brahman-knowledge.
advaita.ins: The three Vedas build three ladders: earth, sky, heaven. But OM goes beyond all three. It reaches what the ladders can't — the silent, ageless, deathless, fearless Absolute. The Vedas take you far. OM takes you all the way.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'शान्तम्-अजरम्-अमृतम्-अभयम्-परम्' — ये भगवान् के पाँच गुण (attributes) हैं। ओंकार इन सभी गुणों-सहित भगवान् का ध्यान-माध्यम (meditation-vehicle) है। विद्वान् (भक्त) ओंकार से भगवान् की सम्पूर्णता (fullness) को प्राप्त करता है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'śānta-ajara-amṛta-abhaya-para' — these are five attributes of the Lord. OM is the meditation-vehicle for the Lord with all these attributes. The vidvān (devotee) through OM reaches the Lord's fullness.
vishisht.ins: Five words paint the portrait of the Supreme: peaceful, ageless, deathless, fearless, supreme. That's who you're reaching when you chant OM with full understanding. Not a vague energy — a Person with these five marks.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'शान्तम्-अजरम्-अमृतम्-अभयम्-परम्' — ये चेतना के अन्तिम लक्ष्य (ultimate goal) के पाँच लक्षण हैं: शान्ति (peace beyond agitation), शाश्वतता (eternity beyond time), अमरत्व (immortality beyond death), निर्भयता (fearlessness beyond duality), और पारगामिता (transcendence beyond all limits)। ओंकार इस लक्ष्य का ध्वनि-स्वरूप (sound-form) है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'śānta-ajara-amṛta-abhaya-para' — five marks of the ultimate goal of consciousness: peace beyond agitation, eternity beyond time, immortality beyond death, fearlessness beyond duality, and transcendence beyond all limits. OM is the sound-form of this goal.
aurobindo.ins: Five words, five negations of everything that makes existence painful: agitation → peace; aging → timelessness; death → immortality; fear → fearlessness; limitation → the supreme. OM is the sound that carries you from the first column to the second.

dp.q: 🔍 The five attributes of Brahman in this verse
dp.a: The closing verse describes Brahman through five attributes, each negating a feature of conditioned existence: (1) Śānta (शान्त) — Peaceful: Brahman is beyond all agitation (vikṣepa). In saṁsāra, the mind is constantly disturbed — by desire, aversion, restlessness. Brahman is the source of all peace — not the peace of exhaustion but the peace of fullness. The Māṇḍūkya (7) uses this word to describe turīya: 'śāntaṁ śivam advaitam' — peaceful, auspicious, non-dual. (2) Ajara (अजर) — Ageless: Brahman does not age or decay. Everything in creation moves from birth to decay to death. Brahman is beyond this sequence — it is kāla-atīta (beyond time). The body ages because it is in time; the Self does not age because it is not in time. (3) Amṛta (अमृत) — Immortal: Brahman is deathless. Not 'living forever' (that would still be within time) but beyond the category of death. The Kaṭha (1.2.18) says: 'The Self is not born, nor does it die.' (4) Abhaya (अभय) — Fearless: Brahman is free from fear. Fear arises from duality — from the perception that there is something 'other' that could threaten you. The Bṛhadāraṇyaka (1.4.2) explains: 'Fear arises from a second entity.' Since Brahman is non-dual, there is no 'other' — hence no fear. The Taittirīya (2.7) says: 'When one finds the fearless foundation in the Invisible, Bodiless, Undefined, Un-based — then one has reached fearlessness.' (5) Para (पर) — Supreme: Brahman is the highest reality — there is nothing beyond it, nothing above it. It is the ultimate ground of everything that exists.

Question 5 of the Prashna Upanishad presents a complete teaching on OM-meditation in seven mantras: Mantra 1 — The question: Satyakāma asks: what world does the lifelong OM-meditator reach? Mantra 2 — The framework: Pippalāda reveals that OM encompasses both para (higher) and apara (lower) Brahman. The depth of meditation determines which is reached. Mantra 3 — One mātrā (A): meditation on A alone → quick rebirth on earth with spiritual qualities (tapas, brahmacharya, śraddhā). Led by the Ṛg Veda. Mantra 4 — Two mātrās (A+U): meditation on A+U → ascent to soma-loka (lunar world), experience of vibhūti (divine glory), but eventual return (punar āvartate). Led by the Yajur Veda. Mantra 5 — Three mātrās (A+U+M): meditation on the complete OM → liberation from sin (snake-skin simile), ascent to brahma-loka, vision of the Supreme Person (parāt-para puruṣa). Led by the Sāma Veda. No return. Mantra 6 — The integration principle: separate mātrās are 'mortal'; only the unified OM, rightly practised in all three domains (external, internal, intermediate), makes the knower unshakeable. Mantra 7 — The culmination: OM is the sole vehicle to the ultimate Brahman — śānta, ajara, amṛta, abhaya, para. The seers know this; the knower reaches this through OM. The teaching's structure: three ascending levels (earth → moon → Brahman) mirroring three Vedas (Ṛg → Yajur → Sāma), three mātrās (A → U → M), and three cosmic regions (bhūḥ → bhuvaḥ → svaḥ). The integration principle (mantra 6) transcends all three levels.
